message:
Every upgrade shows on the car, the boot shows what it carries, and a paint shop

Eight parts, three visible levels each, growing: a pipe bumper to a
bull bar to a toothed plough; door plates to roof plates to mesh and a
riveted bonnet; a scoop to a side pipe to a blower with stacks; wider
tyres to knobbly to mud tyres that spray while sliding; one nitro
bottle to two to a tank with feed lines (nitro is a new JM part: tank
+25% and refill +15% a level); lexan to bare doors and a cage to primer
and a bucket seat; a red caliper to drilled discs to bonnet ducts.
Missiles ride as roof tubes, mines as a box off the tail, oil as a
drum behind the rear glass. The paint shop sells eight worn colours
and six liveries per car, saved with the car. The garage and the shop
show the car as it is; make lineup has a row per part.

The first races are winnable in the starting car: stock rivals, drivers that start poor

Why the rivals had better cars: the field gained a part a race, so by
the fourth folk race their cars lapped Kiviaho 2.1 s faster than a
stock Tauno (2.6 s at the final), and Marko's van weighed 1.44 to 1.90
against the Tauno's 1.25. Now the folk-class field drives stock cars
until the final, where it has a ram bar and an engine; what grows is
the driver, through the event's share of their skill (fieldSkill, 0.7
at the first race to 1.1 at the final), and Marko's van weighs what
the Tauno weighs. The bot's skill now bites: corner margin 0.25 + 0.75
x skill (was 0.45 + 0.55), throttle 0.45 + 0.55 x skill, so a folk
rival laps 40 to 45 s where the learnt bot laps 32; C, B and A skills
moved up to stay where they were. The proof is in sim-check: a bot at
0.65 of its corner margin (37.2 s a lap, the thumb that has not learnt
the car) wins the first two folk races from every grid by 7 to 13 s,
is never last in the class, and the final is a fight. The folk class's
view checks are measured with that driver. The tow clock resets like
the check does, on 3 m of forward progress only.

Turning the phone no longer breaks the view

On iOS Safari the resize fires while the canvas still measures the old
layout, and nothing comes once the layout has settled, so the canvas
kept the old device pixels and the camera the old aspect: the race was
drawn stretched after a turn. Reproduced on an emulated iPhone by
freezing the canvas's measured size for 300 ms across the turn: the
canvas stayed 786x1318 on a 659x393 screen and the view aspect stayed
0.60 against 1.68. Now the game loop asks the renderer every frame
whether the canvas still measures what it was sized to and resizes
before drawing when it does not, and an orientation change schedules
two late resizes. scripts/rotate-check.mjs (make rotate-check) turns
the phone mid-race and in the menus both ways with that stale layout
and asserts the canvas, the camera's aspect, the dash and the pedal.

The wall has trees on it: a car can no longer sit stuck on open grass

The physics stops a car 10 m from the road and at a shortcut's verge,
but the forest was planted from a metre beyond that line, every 4.5 m
with gaps and some trees drawn at half size, so the owner sat at
0 km/h on open grass against a wall nothing showed. A probe found 224
such points on Kiviaho. Now a tree stands on every 2.6 m of the wall
line and of every lane's edge, and the forest grows behind it. A car
under walking pace counts as stalled, so the back-out and the tow fire
while it rocks against the wall, and the tow clock counts forward
progress only, so rocking over the mark does not restart it. scripts/
stuck-check.mjs (make stuck-check) drives the owner's spot on the
iPhone landscape layout with the thumb controls live, four ways, and
asserts the car frees itself within 4 s.

No more wedged cars, a faster game, and jumps that are the track: rivers and crests

The owner got stuck at the hairpin every race: the kicker on the
diagonal threw the car into the trees nose first, and the throttle
held it there at 0 km/h. The kicker is gone, a wedged car backs itself
out after 1.5 s, and the marshals tow a car still stalled off the road
after 4 s, with a tape toast. sim-check asserts no car sits off the
road more than 4 s; the headless repro went from 7 stuck runs in 252
to none. Every car has 30% more pull and 20% more top speed, the bot
takes bends at a span of 12 m instead of 30, and JM laps drop from 35
to 32 s. The planked kickers are replaced by terrain: a river the road
jumps from a bank (Kiviaho's ford, and Hirvisuo's bottom straight) and
a crest on each start straight. A car clears the river from about
70 km/h and drops into the water below that, splashes, and drives out.
touch-check takes PORT for when another repo holds its default.

The wild cast: a tractor, a monster truck, a bus, a snowplough lorry, a hearse, a Niva and the mopoauto

Cars that are all cars is not variety. Marko now drives a Valmet
tractor in C (slow, turns on a dime, mass x1.8, shoves anything), a
monster truck in B (balloon tyres, every shunt spins the victim) and a
plough lorry in A (the blade is a built-in ram level 3). Tapsa drives
the mopoauto in JM, a Niva in C and a country bus in B (7.5 m, mass
x3, a wall). Jorma drives a hearse in A. The dealer sells the Niva and
the tractor in C, the monster in B, the hearse in A, red with a number.
The sim needed damage by the root of the mass, so a tractor does not
wreck a C car in two knocks, and a tow after 8 s stalled off the road.
Two CarDef fields: offroad and spinOnShunt. The C career check pools
both tracks, since the old one passed by luck.

The first race readable and winnable: a wider camera that looks down the road, pace notes, visible damage, tiny JM boxes, rivals that are crap at the start

The owner could not see where the road went, could not see damage,
started in a huge saloon, and lost to rivals at the bot's ceiling. The
camera shows fourteen cars across and leads along the track, not the
velocity. A co-driver calls the next bend: a stencil arrow with 1 to 6
(src/game/notes.ts), from 2.5 s out. Damage stages start at 10 with a
hanging bumper and a smashed lamp, and every hit flashes the car. The
career starts in Fiat 500 sized boxes (JM 2.8 to 3.2 m) and each class
is a size up to A at 5 m. Rivals have a skill per class, JM at 0.3 to
0.4, with a wobble, late braking, a fumbled oil drop and a spray that
scale with how bad they are; sim-check asserts the player wins every
JM race by 3 s and does not win every A race.

Every car is its own: nine bodies, rivals in their own vehicles, upgrades on the car

The cars all looked the same, three times over: the rivals drove the
player's class car with one of three near-identical sedans, and the
player's four cars were all red 4 m boxes. Now there are nine bodies in
Hill Climb Racing's chunky proportions inside the game's worn palette:
saloon, hatch, coupe, rally, estate brick, Beetle, van with a ladder,
pickup with a load, and a microcar. Every rival has a signature vehicle
per class (Jorma's blues, Marko's yellow bricks and vans, Tapsa's white
Beetle and the mopoauto), with its own name, colour, livery and number;
pace still comes from the class car. The player's cars keep red but
each has its own livery and number, and the parts show: a ram bar that
grows into a plough, riveted plates then mesh, barrels on the bonnet,
knobbly tyres, a scoop and pipes. make lineup renders every vehicle on
one sheet; the grid never seats two of a kind.

Kiviaho rebuilt for the first ten seconds: two kickers, an early ford, a shortcut through the forest; Hirvisuo gets a kicker and a ford

A shortcut is data on the track (TrackDef.shortcuts): a lane through the
trees along an open polyline with a width and a surface. Track drives it as a
Lane with its own arc length; the walls are the union of the road's verge and
the lanes' (an impulse at the corner that went in, toward whichever is nearer),
the surface under an axle is the lane's inside it, no trees grow in it, the
ground bakes it as a worn two-track and the minimap dashes it. The bot takes a
lane when told to and as Jorma when well behind the player, slows for the
mouth at the grass's pace, and backs out of a lane wall with the wheel turned
so the nose comes round; a stall now counts going nowhere, not standing still,
so a car rubbing a wall reverses too.

Kiviaho is 680 m around a bigger hairpin: a 0.9 m kicker on the start
straight, the ford right after the first sweeper, a 0.7 m kicker on the
diagonal, the grass lane across the hairpin's inside. sim-check flies every
kicker with every car at racing speed and lands it on the road, crosses every
ford, and drives every shortcut: it must save time and not a free lap (0.6 to
0.9 s a lap for the bot). make drive-log takes the first kicker by touch. The
B licence target is re-read off the longer lap.

in B; the gun part's first level is the gun. The ram bar is its own part. Five
JM events, prizes by the rule in docs/progression.md. Save v2 starts over.

The car is a rigid body: impulses at the contact, a tyre that lets go, surfaces and height

Cars are boxes that meet box against box and push the trees back at
the corner that went in, with an impulse at the contact point: a
glancing tree hit slides along at 84% of its speed, a hit off the
middle turns the other car, bodies never sink in. The tyre falls off
smoothly past its peak; caster, traction control, a rear spin guard
and slide-only yaw damping stand in for the throttle the thumb lacks,
so a slide holds and straightens and a pedal stab turns a hairpin.
Three substeps a frame.

Surfaces are data per track patch (gravel, tarmac, grass, mud, water,
ice) read per axle, and a car has a height: a jump throws it, the air
has no grip, a crooked landing scrubs speed. The old model plays at
?physics=old for one release.

physics-check asserts it in make check. The blast kick and the
catch-up were re-measured so the race stays on screen; sim-check runs
all six grid orders. ADR 0003.

Installable: an icon in the game's style, a fuller manifest, offline play through a generated service worker

The home screen icon was a red brick on a grey strip. It is now the
race in one tile under the game's low sun: a worn red rally car with
its stripes and roof number, dust behind it, a gravel road through
straw, a spruce with its long shadow; the car sits inside the maskable
safe zone. Sizes: 512 and 192 (any and maskable), 180 for iOS, 32 for
the tab. The manifest gets an id, display_override, lang and category.
The build writes sw.js with the list of its own files: hashed assets
from the cache first, everything else network first with the cache as
the fallback, Vary ignored because module scripts carry an Origin.
scripts/pwa-check.mjs (make pwa-check) reads the manifest, loads every
icon at its declared size, waits for the worker's cache, and reloads
the game with the network off.

Steering: a response curve and a longer swing, so a nudge is a correction

On the phone a small thumb move turned far too much and the car could
not be held straight: full lock was 70 px, linear. Now the thumb has a
4 px dead zone, the swing to full lock is 110 px, and the response is
a power curve (1.7): a 20 px nudge gives 4% of lock, where it gave 29%,
so at 72 km/h it yaws 6 degrees a second instead of 43. The sim and
the bot are untouched; the curve lives in input.ts. touch-check asserts
the nudge.

The look, polished: ragged spruce, straw without a repeat, feathered road edges, drawn pickups, half the frame cost

Spruce crowns are overlapping ragged lobes in eight shapes and three
sizes; the straw is clumps placed from world hashes with bare and damp
patches at a larger scale and wheel tracks outside the bends; every
band along the road ends in a wandering seam of dabs and tufts; sparks
are hot streaks, hits throw dark dust, the wreck fire is flame tongues
over a smoke column that leans downwind; pickups are a jerrycan, a
cash bundle, a spanner, a missile and a mine with an amber bracket;
low verge life inside the band. The haze, grade and vignette are one
overlay drawn 1:1, the zoom snaps so ground chunks copy on whole
pixels, the minimap is cached: portrait draw 22 ms to 11 ms headless.

The chrome: a rally dash and a paddock sheet, stencil type, soot and amber

The menus and HUD were system font, a green gradient, pill buttons
and emoji against the new frame. Now they share its palette: soot
panels with grain, Big Shoulders Stencil for the name, digits and the
big buttons, the plain face where a stencil L would read as I.I,
segmented amber lamps for damage, nitro and heat, inline SVG glyphs
for the ammo and switches, a ribbed pedal and a three-spoke wheel,
tape-strip toasts, a riveted plate on the title, a rally plate in the
garage, a timing sheet and a paper receipt on the result, a stamp for
the record. The icon is redrawn to match. No emoji, no green.

The look: a low August sun, long shadows, gravel and straw, worn nineties cars

Mad Max the movie, not Toy Story (docs/design.md). One light from the
upper left, baked into the car sprites per heading and into the ground
as hard static shadows. The ground is baked in chunks: dry straw, a
ditch and verge, polished gravel with ruts and loose stones. The
roadside comes from the track: near-black spruce, birch, juniper and
boulders, posts, bales, a barn with a rusting hulk, a power line, two
crowds with flags. Cars have bonnets, pillars, flared arches, two-tone
liveries and roof numbers, mud, and damage in three stages with smoke.
Dust hangs and tints, a haze and a warm grade sit over the frame. The
sights, cone and minimap are stencil.

Rivals that fight: grudges, blocking, the leader draws fire, and wrecking pays more than the road

Burnout's hostility arrow and Death Rally's bounty: a car remembers who
hit it and leans on them, punts them from behind, blocks them when they
come up, and the guns prefer them. The race leader counts as a grudge
to everyone behind. Each driver has an aggression: Marko brawls, Jorma
drives, Tapsa flinches. The wreck bounty goes to 200 per class and a
spinning ram pays 25 on the spot; road cash halves, so a race driven
hard pays more than one driven round the pickups. sim-check prints the
fight and asserts it.

Arcade grip on the real model: two g, more lock at speed

At 1.25 g the car still read as understeering on the phone. The limit
was the push, not the balance: at 72 km/h a 1.2 g car cannot turn
tighter than 34 m and the hairpins are 16 m. The tyres now hold about
two g, the lock halves at 50 m/s instead of 32, the throttle's cost on
the rear is larger so power still loosens it. Measured neutral through
the range; laps are back where the first version had them and the bot
is clean in every car. Licence targets follow.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_0139QXLWGDwLStv9oTVPV53o

A neutral car that rotates at the limit, and a bot that can catch it

The first cut of the bicycle model pushed: rear grip above the front,
a boxy yaw inertia, the throttle's cost shared by both axles. Now the
rear has 0.9 of the front's grip, the yaw inertia is 0.75 of a box, the
throttle's cost lands on the rear only and the brakes' on the front, and
the tyres have a notch more grip. Measured with a handling table rather
than by feel: at 15 m/s and a third of lock the Kortteli turns at the
kinematic rate at 1.2 g with the rear just past its peak. The bot
counter-steers a rear slip past the peak and holds a little throttle
instead of braking while the tail is out; without that it spun every
car. The Kiila's pull is trimmed. Licence targets follow the new laps.
The research notes record the settled numbers.

The car is a bicycle model: real tyres, weight transfer, a friction circle

Marco Monster's model replaces the hand-written one: a slip angle per
axle, a cornering force that saturates at grip times load, yaw from the
axles' torque about the centre of gravity, load to the front under
braking, and a friction circle so braking and driving cost cornering
grip. Drive and braking are capped by the tyres. The yaw rate blends to
the kinematic bicycle at walking pace. Nothing adds yaw by hand any more,
so a sliding car no longer does donuts; a car asked for too much plows,
and the tail comes round under braking because the rear is light.

The bot steers by the yaw rate it wants through the wheelbase, brakes to
the speed a bend allows from grip and radius, and brakes when it is
running wide. Laps are about a third longer; the licence targets follow.
ADR 0002 records the decision.

Combat racer: tyres that let go, nitro, automatic guns, ramming, wrecks, pickups

The race half rebuilt on Death Rally, Burnout and Mad Max, after a look
at what those games are loved for. The tyres pull the slide back up to
a grip limit and past it the car slides with yaw inertia; the one pedal
brakes and loosens the rear, so braking into a corner swings the tail;
grass is loose rather than slow. A tap is nitro, a burst from a tank
that drifting, ramming and above all wrecking fill. Every weapon fires
itself: the machine gun at a car in the cone ahead with heat, a missile
once the lock has held, a mine when a car is right behind; the guns
stay quiet for three seconds after the lights. A shunt hurts the car
that was hit, the heavier and armoured car wins, a hard one spins. At
100 damage a car is a wreck that burns and comes back on the centreline
half fixed, and the car that did it is paid a bounty on the spot. Cash,
nitro, wrenches, missiles and mines lie on the road and grow back.
Armour and the gun are parts; mines replace oil in the armoury.

Skid marks on a kept layer, tracers, sights on the target, sparks,
nitro flame, burning wrecks, screen shake, toasts for cash and wrecks.
sim-check races the field armed and asserts the guns fire, the cars
slide and everyone finishes; the touch check runs a solo licence lap
and places the car on the straight before each drag.

Guns: missiles, oil slicks, damage and repairs; the steering made visible

Super Cars II's half. A tap fires a missile that homes on the nearest
car ahead and spins what it hits; the oil button leaves a slick behind
that spins whoever drives in. Hits, trees and hard contact add damage
that costs pace during the race and a repair after it, taken from the
prize. The armoury in the garage sells both by the shot, carried from
race to race; a new career starts with four missiles and three slicks.
Opponents shoot back from the second event of a class on, and back out
of a tree when stuck. sim-check races the field armed and asserts
everyone finishes, then unarmed and asserts the order follows skill.

The steering is visible now: the front wheels turn on the car, and a
steering wheel at the bottom centre turns with it, bright while the
thumb is down. Weapon buttons at the bottom right carry the ammo counts,
the damage bar sits under the clock.

Three car bodies, a brake pedal, and reverse

Each class's car has its own body: the hatchback is boxy with a big
rear window, the coupe long and low with a lip spoiler, the rally car
